etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English glas, from Old English glæs, from Proto-West Germanic *glas, from Proto-Germanic *glasą, possibly related to Proto-Germanic *glōaną (“to shine”) (compare glow), and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵʰel- (“to shine, shimmer, glow”). Cognate with West Frisian glês, Dutch glas, Low German Glas, German Glas, Swedish glas, Icelandic gler.

definitions.definition: (usually uncountable) An amorphous solid, often transparent substance, usually made by melting silica sand with various additives (for most purposes, a mixture of soda, potash and lime is added).

quote.citation: 2013 September-October, Henry Petroski, “The Evolution of Eyeglasses”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: The ability of a segment of a glass sphere to magnify whatever is placed before it was known around the year 1000, when the spherical segment was called a reading stone, essentially what today we might term a frameless magnifying glass or plain glass paperweight.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable, by extension) Any amorphous solid (one without a regular crystal lattice).
(countable) A vessel from which one drinks, especially one made of glass, plastic, or similar translucent or semi-translucent material.
(metonymically) The quantity of liquid contained in such a vessel.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter II, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Here was my chance. I took the old man aside, and two or three glasses of Old Crow launched him into reminiscence.

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, chapter III, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: At half-past nine on this Saturday evening, the parlour of the Salutation Inn, High Holborn, contained most of its customary visitors. […] In former days every tavern of repute kept such a room for its own select circle, a club, or society, of habitués, who met every evening, for a pipe and a cheerful glass.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Glassware.
A mirror.

quote.citation: 1599, Thomas Dekker, Old Fortunatus, Act III, Scene 1, J.M. Dent & Co., 1904, p. 67,[1]
quote.text: […]  for what lady can abide to love a spruce silken-face courtier, that stands every morning two or three hours learning how to look by his glass, how to speak by his glass, how to sigh by his glass, how to court his mistress by his glass? I would wish him no other plague, but to have a mistress as brittle as glass.

quote.text: Beholding her charms in the glaſs, ſhe wandered over a wilderneſs of vain fancies.

quote.text: As of old, he took down his portable glass hanging on a nail, and carefully wiping it, replaced it in its case.

definitions.definition: A magnifying glass or telescope.

quote.text: Haviers, or stags which have been gelded when young, have no horns, as is well known, and in the early part of the stalking season, when seen through a glass, might be mistaken for hummels  […]

quote.text: He got a good glass for six hundred dollars.His new job gave him leisure for star-gazing.Often he bid me come and have a lookUp the brass barrel, velvet black inside,At a star quaking in the other end.

definitions.definition: (basketball, colloquial) The backboard.
(ice hockey) The clear, protective screen surrounding a hockey rink.
(sports) A barrier made of solid, transparent material.
A barometer.

quote.citation: 1938, Louis MacNeice, “Bagpipe Music”, in The Earth Compels‎[2], page 59:
quote.text: The glass is falling hour by hour, the glass will fall for ever / But if you break the bloody glass you won’t hold up the weather.

definitions.definition: (attributive, in names of species) Transparent or translucent.
(obsolete) An hourglass.

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: Were my Wiues Liuer / Infected (as her life) ſhe would not liue / The running of one Glaſſe.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, photography, informal) Lenses, considered collectively.
(countable, now rare) Synonym of window or pane, particularly in vehicles.

quote.citation: 1790, Jane Austen, “Love and Freindship”, in Juvenilia:
quote.text: [N]o sooner had we entered Holbourn than letting down one of the Front Glasses I enquired of every decent-looking Person that we passed ‘If they had seen my Edward?’

quote.text: Ladies are usually conveyed about Calcutta, or any where for short distances, in a kind of palanquin, called a boҫhah... Its deep shape, and its seat, much resemble the [English sedan chair]; but having two doors, one on each side, with one window in front, as well as a small one behind, all furnished with Venetians and glasses, give it, in those respects, some claim to alliance with the [chariot].

definitions.definition: (transitive) To fit with glass; to glaze.
(transitive) To enclose in glass.

definitions.definition: (transitive) Clipping of fibreglass. To fit, cover, fill, or build, with fibreglass-reinforced resin composite (fiberglass).
(transitive, UK, colloquial) To strike (someone), particularly in the face, with a drinking glass with the intent of causing injury.

quote.citation: 2003, Mark Sturdy, Pulp page 139:

definitions.definition: (transitive, science fiction) To bombard an area with such intensity (by means of a nuclear bomb, fusion bomb, etc) as to melt the landscape into glass.

quote.citation: 2003, Eric Nylund, Halo: First Strike, New York: Del Rey, →ISBN, page 155:
quote.text: “The Covenant don’t ‘miss’ anything when they glass a planet,” the Master Chief replied.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To view through an optical instrument such as binoculars.

quote.citation: 2000, Ben D. Mahaffey, 50 Years of Hunting and Fishing, page 95:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To smooth or polish (leather, etc.), by rubbing it with a glass burnisher.
(archaic, reflexive) To reflect; to mirror.

quote.citation: 1856, John Lothrop Motley, The Rise of the Dutch Republic. A History. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make glassy.

quote.text: Not only were his eyes averted from mine, but they were glassed to an uncanny degree.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become glassy.

quote.text: Bourez had timed it perfectly: a wind that was forecast for the morning began to stir just after his arrival and the sea glassed off for a brief period before the waves grew bigger and bigger.
